statement: Agricola’s 1556 account presents human, animal and hydraulic mine-work choices together and includes repairable components and site access among practical considerations.

sources.locator: Book II pp. 31–33; Book VI pp. 171–185, especially replacement teeth p. 173 and staged pump pp. 184–185
sources.supports: Documents explicit technical choices and maintenance provisions in the treatise.

counterevidence: Texts and illustrations may describe exemplary arrangements rather than common practice.
inference_limits: Supports existence of described techniques and stated criteria, not measured prevalence, profitability or a universal choice rule.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: In sixteenth- and seventeenth-century central European mining, rod transmission extended the use of waterpower to pumps distant from the stream; non-steam engineering continued to change.

sources.supports: Compares crank-driven pumps, remote rods, balanced transmission and later depictions.

counterevidence: Introduction dates vary; some depicted machinery is ambiguous. Some applications remained tied to local hydrology.
inference_limits: No region-wide diffusion denominator. Adequate hydraulics delaying German steam adoption is a further hypothesis, not established by this claim.

test.mechanism_chain: Remote hydraulic resource -> construct rod linkage -> mechanical power reaches distant pumps -> expanded site choice.
test.strongest_rival: Static post-Agricola mining would predict little relevant configuration change; a weaker rival accepts change but denies cost advantage.
test.discriminating_observation: Later mechanisms and installations absent from Agricola distinguish change; operating accounts are needed for cost advantage.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read Agricola and Multhauf (IND-S01/S02); latter compares remote rod/ balanced transmission and later depictions.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Configuration change is supported; diffusion rate and net advantage remain unresolved.

statement: Nuvolari’s Cornish comparison links early Newcomen use to tolerable fuel costs and the uptake of more fuel-efficient Watt engines to the expense of imported coal in Cornwall.

sources.supports: Contrasts fuel-intensive atmospheric engines and Cornish demand for fuel economy; documents Boulton and Watt deployments.

counterevidence: Engine cost, drainage needs, labour, maintenance and royalties also entered investment decisions.
inference_limits: An historically supported pathway, not isolated identification of coal prices; cheap energy did not characterise every successful steam market.

test.mechanism_chain: High fuel use plus local fuel price -> investor comparison -> fuel-saving design becomes more attractive -> Cornish deployment.
test.strongest_rival: Drainage demand or capital/engineering availability alone could yield deployment without a coal-price mechanism.
test.discriminating_observation: Matched engine choices and total costs across sites with comparable drainage but different delivered coal prices.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S03 pp. 10–12: coalfield/Cornish fuel contrast and condenser deployments; no matched-site experiment acquired.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Engine capability, finance and demand differ with geography.

statement: From 1811, Cornish engine reporting made performance and practices comparable across installations; Nuvolari interprets this information sharing and overlapping investment as supports for incremental improvement.

sources.supports: Describes Lean’s reporting, engineering competition and cost-book ownership.

counterevidence: High-pressure designs and new investment arrived concurrently; a slack period followed patent expiry before reporting began.
inference_limits: Does not estimate the reporting effect separately from investment, engineers, fuel prices or design changes; original engine reports not directly audited.

test.mechanism_chain: Comparable public engine reports -> engineer comparison and reputation -> incremental changes -> improved duty.
test.strongest_rival: New high-pressure designs and investment alone predict improving duty, even without disclosure.
test.discriminating_observation: Within comparable investment/design cohorts, reporting exposure predicts improvement; evidence of actual copying strengthens transmission.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S03 pp. 14–20: reporting intent, public comparisons, changing duty and shared ownership; original report series not audited.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Reporting, design, investment and district growth coincide.

statement: Watt’s fuel-saving royalties and patent enforcement generated documented conflict in Cornwall; Nuvolari argues that broad exclusion also obstructed rival steam development.

sources.supports: Describes royalty formula, disputes, Hornblower and post-expiry withdrawal of Cornish orders.

counterevidence: Patents and royalties may also have financed development and dissemination; cessation of monopoly was not followed by immediate technical progress.
inference_limits: The direction and magnitude of net patent effects remain disputed. Distinguish the documented dispute from the author’s wider innovation judgement.

test.mechanism_chain: Broad patent enforcement -> restricted rival development -> delayed adoption of alternatives.
test.strongest_rival: Patent rents finance development and disclosure; litigation may protect appropriation rather than reduce total innovation.
test.discriminating_observation: Blocked independently workable designs and post-restriction improvement controlling for engineering capacity; also evidence of R&D financed by rents.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S03 pp. 12–14: Hornblower dispute, royalties, order cessation and subsequent slack period.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Dispute is stronger evidence than net innovation effect; expiry alone did not produce immediate progress.

statement: In Crafts’s January 2002 reconstruction, steam contributed less than 0.01 percentage points per year to British labour-productivity growth before 1830, with a larger later contribution including railways.

sources.supports: Reports growth-accounting estimates and their stock/share assumptions.

counterevidence: Early engine stocks are incomplete and unmeasured enabling effects may not be captured by aggregate accounting.
inference_limits: An estimate from the inspected version, not a timeless consensus or evidence that steam was unnecessary at individual sites. No cross-era forecast is made.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: Jonell and colleagues reconstruct unused waterpower potential across much of Britain alongside local constraints around Greater Manchester, and describe supplementary steam use in water-powered mills.

sources.locator: “Impact on the British textile industry”; hydropower and mill-census methods; abstract
sources.supports: Supports geographical heterogeneity and mixed-power operation.

counterevidence: Reservoir construction, ownership, transmission and industrial location could alter usable supply; theoretical national potential is not economically deployable capacity.
inference_limits: Partial-text inspection only; underlying model and supplements not rerun. Local scarcity does not identify why factories originally clustered there.

test.mechanism_chain: Local dependable water constraints -> mill seeks extra power -> steam supplement/replacement -> capacity expansion.
test.strongest_rival: Labour access/control or agglomeration could favour steam despite adequate water; national abundance predicts no shortage only if local access is ignored.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable mills/sites with usable flow versus scarce flow, plus seasonal output and expansion decisions.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S05 impact/method sections: local Manchester constraint alongside national potential and supplementary steam; compared IND-S06 coordination abstract.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Industrial clustering partly creates scarcity; reservoir costs, rights and labour conditions unresolved.

statement: Malm argues that large proposed reservoir schemes in the 1820s–1830s failed partly because their collective financing and coordination requirements conflicted with manufacturers’ arrangements.

sources.supports: Explicitly attributes non-realisation of reservoir schemes to coordination and collective funding.

counterevidence: Physical reliability, projected demand, land rights and cost assumptions are alternative or interacting explanations.
inference_limits: Abstract-only evidence: claim is about the author’s interpretation, not an independent finding that water was consistently cheaper or every proposed scheme feasible.

test.mechanism_chain: Shared reservoir requires funding and allocation -> manufacturers cannot coordinate -> proposed expansion not built.
test.strongest_rival: Projects may be physically unreliable or financially unattractive even under feasible collective governance.
test.discriminating_observation: Scheme correspondence and cost/flow evidence showing viable projects blocked specifically by coordination, compared with realised schemes.
test.evidence_sought_found: Searched full article; only IND-S06 author abstract acquired. It explicitly makes the coordination claim; scheme-level evidence not found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Both rivals fit non-building. Weak-access claim retained only as attributed hypothesis.

statement: Allen’s explanation assigns British mechanisation to labour being expensive relative to capital and energy, and subsequent wider diffusion to improvements that reduced other input requirements.

sources.supports: States the factor-price and later engineering-diffusion thesis directly.

counterevidence: Task-specific female wages, regional heterogeneity, skills, markets and political power complicate the aggregate comparison.
inference_limits: Attribution of a hypothesis; introductory excerpt does not validate Allen’s profitability calculations or universal foreign non-viability.

test.mechanism_chain: High relevant labour cost relative to machinery/energy -> expected cost saving -> investment in labour-saving inventions/adoption.
test.strongest_rival: Low-paid spinning labour, quality requirements and skill/market complements could motivate or constrain adoption independently.
test.discriminating_observation: Task- and location-matched wages, output quality and machine payback comparisons before invention, including nonadopters.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read Allen excerpt IND-S07 and archival-pay critique IND-S08; high-wage formulation is clear but spinner wage surge is challenged.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Allen’s underlying calculations and later responses not inspected; international and local wages use different comparisons.

statement: Humphries and Schneider’s reconstructed British hand-spinning pay does not show a general wage surge immediately before the spinning inventions; it challenges including these workers in an undifferentiated high-wage economy.

sources.supports: Documents archival construction, source-type differences and absence of the proposed sharp wage increase.

counterevidence: Cotton data are scarce, fibres and worker populations differ, and daily earnings involve time assumptions; Allen’s later rejoinders are not assessed here.
inference_limits: A challenge to a particular wage premise, not proof that factor prices never mattered or causal identification of quality control as the alternative motive.

test.mechanism_chain: Reconstructed pay by source type does not show the proposed general pre-invention surge -> weakens the proposed general wage-surge premise. This does not identify the marginal labour-cost return to a particular machine or exclude wage incentives.
test.strongest_rival: Samples overrepresent institutional/part-time low-output labour, concealing a high-wage commercial cotton margin.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable full-time commercial cotton spinning records with counts and hours, versus institutional and other fibres.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S08 source definitions, records and regressions: no general surge, source-type gaps, sparse cotton observations; explicit limits preserved.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Wage levels, wage changes, daily earnings, hourly labour costs and returns to a particular machine are different measures. Sparse commercial cotton records and working-time assumptions leave the relevant marginal incentive unresolved; alternative invention motives in IND-S08 remain speculative.

statement: In 1835 Ure publicly advocated factory mechanisation partly as a means to substitute cheaper labour and reduce dependence on independent skilled workers.

sources.locator: extract paragraphs beginning “The principle of the factory system”, “By the infirmity”, and “In the infancy of mechanical engineering”; compiler original-page ranges 20–23, 29–31
sources.supports: Records contemporary managerial advocacy for skill substitution and tractability.

counterevidence: Skilled mechanics and machine operatives remained necessary; Ure is a partisan advocate whose welfare claims are not corroborated by this extract.
inference_limits: Shows a stated aspiration, not universal employer intention, successful complete deskilling or demonstrated worker benefit.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: Kelly and Ó Gráda trace a pathway from instrument-making skill and precision measurement to complex textile machinery and the machine tools needed for repeated production and replacement parts.

sources.supports: Identifies skill transfer, gauges and exact tools, and the demand for reproducible wearing components.

counterevidence: The jenny and atmospheric engine could use less elaborate capabilities; cross-country tool histories have other routes and political contingencies.
inference_limits: A historically supported pathway rather than a universal prerequisite; no independent causal effect of national skill endowment is estimated.

test.mechanism_chain: Precision craft/measurement capabilities -> reproducible complicated components -> machinery supply and replacement -> sustained industrial use.
test.strongest_rival: Demand/capital expansion alone induces both tool skill and machinery; capabilities could be an outcome rather than prior constraint.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated personnel/tool transfers preceding new workable designs and matched sites with demand but missing skills.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S10 sections 2.1–2.3: named instrument/mechanic transfers, valve making and machine-tool/parts account; also simpler early artifacts acknowledged.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Demand and supply reinforce one another; broad national claims lack an exogenous comparison.

statement: Broadberry and Gupta’s reconstruction makes the timing of Lancashire’s competitive gains depend on raw-cotton and transport costs as well as wages and uneven productivity advances across spinning and weaving.

sources.supports: Reconstructs comparative wages, productivity proxies, raw cotton prices and market-specific delivery costs.

counterevidence: Indian productivity stagnation is assumed for key intervals, and household earnings and labour units are not directly comparable; political market access remains a rival/complement.
inference_limits: Applies to the inspected 2005 model and reconstruction, not directly measured productivity for all Indian textiles or proof of tariffs’ irrelevance.

test.mechanism_chain: Productivity rises unevenly and cotton/freight costs change -> relative delivered cost shifts -> merchants source differently -> competitive reversal.
test.strongest_rival: Colonial policy and coercive market access could drive the same trade shifts without equivalent cost advantage.
test.discriminating_observation: Quality-matched delivered costs and shares across markets with different policy but similar transport, before and after price changes.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S11 pp. 16–25 and conclusion; compared IND-S13 policy testimony. The cost model includes cotton/freight but assumes some Indian productivity paths.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Policy shapes prices and markets; quality and labour-unit comparability remain incomplete.

statement: Clingingsmith and Williamson propose that pre-1810 Indian textile decline involved domestic political/agricultural shocks, while later decline involved stronger international manufactured-price pressure.

sources.supports: Uses a three-sector model and relative-price evidence to propose two phases.

counterevidence: Regional political histories and data are uneven; colonial intervention, quality changes and capital constraints are not independently isolated by these prices.
inference_limits: Model assumptions include mobile labour, subsistence-linked pay and initially non-traded grain. This is an interpretation, not exogenous identification of drought or Mughal decline.

test.mechanism_chain: Domestic agricultural/political shock -> dear grain and subsistence-linked nominal wages -> reduced textile competitiveness; later world textile prices add pressure.
test.strongest_rival: Colonial interventions or textile demand shifts could alter prices and employment without the posited agricultural cause.
test.discriminating_observation: District timing: independently measured harvest/drought/conflict shocks preceding wage pressure and textile contraction, including low-shock controls.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S12 model and relative-price/timing argument; no independently identified district treatment comparison found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Modelled labour mobility and wage linkage do causal work; price data alone fit multiple mechanisms.

statement: Inikori argues that Atlantic demand linked to slavery-based commodity production helped form the markets and regional expansion within which British cotton mechanisation developed.

sources.locator: sections I–III, especially section II paragraphs on Lancashire’s wages and Atlantic export sales
sources.supports: Connects regional protoindustry, Atlantic demand and later mechanisation.

counterevidence: Factor prices, domestic demand, engineering and other trading regions also matter; regional wage rankings do not by themselves adjudicate international wage comparisons.
inference_limits: An attributed historical mechanism, not a quantified necessary contribution of slavery to each invention. Export demand is not the same variable as investment finance.

test.mechanism_chain: Slavery-linked Atlantic commodity trade -> expanding markets -> regional protoindustry growth -> investment and mechanisation incentives.
test.strongest_rival: Domestic markets, factor prices or engineering can explain innovation; Atlantic demand might follow rather than precede industrial advantage.
test.discriminating_observation: Regional/sectoral demand exposure preceding investment, with comparable low-exposure producers and separate supply/finance channels.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S13 regional wage/exports sequence and IND-S11 competition account; temporal market linkage found, no isolated necessity test.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Atlantic markets, shipping, wages and political power are reciprocally connected; export shares are not investment causality.

statement: Inikori’s discussion of Charles Grant’s 1821 testimony identifies asymmetric British and Indian tariff power as a contemporary concern alongside improvements in machinery.

sources.locator: section IV, Charles Grant paragraph immediately preceding table 3
sources.supports: Reproduces an explicit contemporary argument about protection at home and political power over Indian imports.

counterevidence: The testimony does not establish a tariff counterfactual for each cloth quality or exclude cost-driven competitive shifts.
inference_limits: Primary testimony is accessed through Inikori’s quotation via Chaudhuri; original parliamentary record not independently inspected. No causal magnitude assigned.

test.mechanism_chain: Imperial tariff authority -> asymmetric protection/import permission -> altered producer choice set and market access.
test.strongest_rival: Productivity and freight advantages alone would produce the same import shift under symmetric sovereignty.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable products under differing tariff regimes and original legislative/merchant records on excluded choices.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read Grant testimony as reproduced in IND-S13 section IV; sought original-record specificity but did not acquire parliamentary source.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Testimony establishes awareness and constrained sovereignty more firmly than the counterfactual trade magnitude.

statement: Japanese mills in the 1890s adapted ring spinning through a package involving cotton imports, mixed fibres, more preparation labour and a changed labour force, rather than merely copying American operating conditions.

sources.supports: Combines order specifications with historical accounts of cotton preparation and workforce change.

counterevidence: Cotton prices, yarn markets and suppliers changed concurrently; order specifications are not direct measurements of realised mill productivity.
inference_limits: Does not establish the separate effect of each component, or that the labour arrangements were freely chosen or beneficial to workers.

test.mechanism_chain: Imported fibre variety plus labour-intensive mixing -> reduced breakage/broader fibre control -> viable rings under Japanese conditions.
test.strongest_rival: Changes in machine design or yarn demand alone could improve performance without preparation reorganisation.
test.discriminating_observation: Within comparable machinery and yarn counts, mixing adoption precedes improved throughput/breakage; costs and work hours measured.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S14 pp. 549–551, order table and contemporary observations: timing of mixed-cotton orders and package change support the pathway.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Order proxies do not independently identify labour, fibres and design; exact realised productivity not observed.

statement: Between 1878 and 1914 mule and ring spinning both continued to improve; Saxonhouse and Wright interpret British mule persistence as a choice supported by skills and product flexibility, not simply stagnant technology.

sources.supports: Documents coexisting technologies, skill requirements and adoption models using changing technical frontiers.

counterevidence: Rings later gained capabilities and mule performance growth slowed; rationality at one time does not demonstrate optimal long-run investment.
inference_limits: Technical specification proxies and nonexperimental firm-choice models do not isolate learning, and the authors’ strong claim about unavoidable British decline is not adopted here.

test.mechanism_chain: Mule-specific skills and continuing machine improvement -> sustained capability -> continued purchases where advantageous.
test.strongest_rival: Entrenched employers/unions or sunk capital produce persistence despite inferior returns.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare realised quality-adjusted profits and best-practice improvements in new mule purchases versus feasible rings, not only old stocks.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S14 performance specifications and choice model: both technologies improve before 1914 and multiple countries buy mules.
test.remaining_ambiguity: New orders weaken a pure obsolete-stock story but may still reflect expectations, omitted costs or institutional constraints.

statement: India supplied the largest number of high-draft machinery orders in Saxonhouse and Wright’s 1929–1933 dataset, a bounded counterexample to equating low wages with non-adoption of labour-saving equipment.

sources.supports: Reports destination ordering and qualifications to the labour-relations explanation.

counterevidence: Order count is not an installed-stock share or necessarily a comparable fraction of each country’s capacity.
inference_limits: Restricted to the supplier dataset and interval; the paper’s proposed male-workforce/labour-relations mechanism remains tentative.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: In late Qing and Republican China, some handweavers combined machine-spun warp with hand-spun weft, and cheaper factory yarn also supported handloom weaving in new districts.

sources.supports: Describes mixed yarn use, Dingxian and geographical expansion of hand weaving.

counterevidence: Hand spinning declined and factory cloth increased its share; hybrid persistence differed by region and product.
inference_limits: Earlier studies underlying Eyferth’s historical background were not independently acquired; no nationwide adoption rate is inferred from the examples.

test.mechanism_chain: Cheap machine yarn -> replace selected spinning inputs -> handloom production retains product functions and expands accessible supply.
test.strongest_rival: General market growth alone may sustain hand weaving; poor households may simply be unable to buy cloth.
test.discriminating_observation: Yarn-price/access changes preceding weaving expansion, with product-level evidence of mixed warp/weft and comparison to inaccessible districts.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S15 pp. 373–374: explicit mixed yarn and named new weaving districts; original local studies not independently acquired.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Price, population, cash and fabric differences interact; mechanism stronger than national quantitative effect.

statement: Eyferth reports that handloom cloth accounted for about 70 percent of China’s cotton textile output in 1934–1936, despite the expansion of factory production.

sources.supports: Provides the bounded period and output denominator for the reported estimate.

counterevidence: Handloom market share was declining and aggregation may mask regional variation; the underlying estimation method was not audited.
inference_limits: An attributed estimate from earlier research, not a newly verified census; cannot equate output share with employment share or household welfare.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: Eyferth documents moral and gendered classifications of textile work in late imperial and Republican China, including reform rhetoric that rendered household female production economically invisible.

sources.supports: Contrasts gendered household ideals, diverse practice and later reformist definitions of productive work.

counterevidence: Actual household divisions were more varied than prescriptive discourse; beliefs alone need not explain persistence when cash, prices and employment differ.
inference_limits: Documents classifications and interpretation, not freely expressed worker preferences. Post-1949 rationing mechanisms are excluded from this pre-1950 case.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: American factory electrification included distinct line-shaft, group-drive and unit-drive arrangements; replacing a prime mover with a motor did not automatically reorganise factory power distribution.

sources.supports: Documents the configurations, early retrofits and the functional differences.

counterevidence: Group drive remained useful in some applications, and older configurations survived beyond the main transition.
inference_limits: The engineering distinction is well documented; it supplies neither an exact date for universal replacement nor proof that all firms benefited from unit drive.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: Devine links effective unit-drive use to compatible machinery, production redesign, utility expansion and application services, with sunk onsite equipment differentiating retrofits from new plants.

sources.locator: pp. 363, 368–371; machine redesign and Detroit Edison paragraphs
sources.supports: Describes indirect production benefits, compatibility constraints and services offered with electricity.

counterevidence: Firms varied in load, process and existing capital; some group-drive choices remained justified. Expanding firms may have selected electrification.
inference_limits: Not causal identification of all postwar productivity gains; worker pace, discretion and welfare are not assessed by the engineering evidence.

test.mechanism_chain: Compatible motors/tools plus redesign and service -> flexible local power -> productive reorganisation -> adoption benefits.
test.strongest_rival: Demand-led expansion or new capital generally causes both redesign and productivity, with motors only accompanying it.
test.discriminating_observation: Matched retrofits/new plants measuring workflow and output before/after, with comparable non-electric new equipment.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S16 configuration history, redesign comments and utility installation services; evidence for needed complements found, no clean experiment.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Selective engineering cases and firm growth can bias productivity interpretation; unit drive not always superior.

statement: Devine reports that electric motors represented roughly one-quarter of US manufacturing mechanical-drive horsepower in 1909 and over half in 1919; he separately infers unit-drive diffusion because comprehensive configuration statistics were unavailable.

sources.supports: Provides the capacity denominator and explains indirect evidence for unit-drive timing.

counterevidence: Installed capacity is not utilisation, output, establishment adoption or the source of electricity generation.
inference_limits: Reuses the bounded historical series, not a reconstructed census; motor adoption must not be counted as complete factory redesign.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.
